summary: A snapshot taken in October 2008 by the IRTF Internet Congestion Control Research Group, surveying congestion control topics covered across the RFC series. It does not change any specification and is meant as a reference and a starting point for noting gaps in IETF standards. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a guidebook listing everything written down so far about how to stop roads from jamming up when too many cars arrive at once.

subtitle: A survey of IETF RFCs that address how the Internet avoids getting overloaded.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs mechanisms to prevent congestion collapse when many flows send data simultaneously, and many different approaches have been published as RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC surveys existing RFCs on congestion control, organizing them by category: architectural guidance, TCP mechanisms, link characteristics, signaling methods, multicast, and guidance for new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: It serves as a reference and starting point for researchers and protocol designers who need to understand the landscape of existing congestion control work.

today: RFC 5783 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a valuable reference for understanding the breadth of congestion control work in the RFC series, though researchers should consult newer RFCs and the literature for recent developments beyond 2008.

sections.title: Overview of Congestion Control
sections.content:
Congestion control is defined as feedback-based adjustment of the rate at which data is sent into the network. Since 1988, it has been essential to the Internet's stability. Although TCP has been the main focus, congestion control is also used by many other applications and protocols.

This RFC takes a snapshot of congestion control topics in the RFC series as of October 2008. It is organized as an annotated bibliography covering topics from host requirements to multicast, architectural guidance, and emerging techniques. The document reflects a two-year consensus-building process by the IRTF Internet Congestion Control Research Group.
sections.eli5: This section says: we need ways to slow down when the network gets crowded, and lots of people have written official rules about this.

sections.title: Architectural Guidance and Foundational RFCs
sections.content:
Several RFCs provide foundational principles and requirements. RFC 1122 mandates that hosts perform congestion control for TCP and leaves it to higher layers for UDP. RFC 2309 recommends Active Queue Management (AQM) in routers and warns of congestion collapse. RFC 2914 (BCP 41) is the IETF's Best Current Practice for congestion control design, emphasizing the need for non-TCP protocols to implement congestion control to prevent collapse.

More recent guidance includes RFC 5033, which specifies when experimental TCP modifications should be published, and RFC 5166, which defines metrics for evaluating congestion control mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Some important rules say: all programs must slow down when the network is busy, and routers should warn before their queues get too full instead of just dropping packets.

sections.title: TCP Congestion Control Mechanisms
sections.content:
TCP's congestion control mechanisms, standardized in RFC 2581 (obsoleting RFC 2001), define algorithms like slow start and congestion avoidance. These were developed by Van Jacobson in 1988 and became universal in TCP implementations. The RFC also surveys extensions for high-speed networks (HighSpeed TCP, Limited Slow-Start) and discusses modifications for improved startup and recovery times.

The TCP Roadmap (RFC 4614) provides a more detailed overview of TCP-specific RFCs, which this document does not replicate. The TCPM Working Group was developing updates to incorporate accumulated knowledge and advance TCP mechanisms on the Standards Track.
sections.eli5: TCP has special rules for how fast to send data: start slow, then speed up if nothing is lost, but slow down immediately if packets disappear.

sections.title: Handling Difficult Network Conditions
sections.content:
Networks with large bandwidth-delay products (like satellite links), high packet loss rates, or unusual link characteristics can break standard congestion control. RFCs address TCP performance over satellite links, wireless networks, networks with errors, and paths with asymmetric capacity. Performance Enhancing Proxies (PEPs), while architecturally questionable, are used in practice for degraded environments.

The Performance Implications of Link Characteristics (PILC) Working Group produced many of these RFCs. While they focus on TCP, the principles apply to other protocols using similar feedback mechanisms, such as SCTP and DCCP with CCID 2.
sections.eli5: Special kinds of networks (like super-long-distance ones) confuse the normal rules, so there are extra tricks to use in those places.

sections.title: Explicit Signaling Between Hosts and Routers
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), standardized in RFC 3168, allows routers to mark packets instead of dropping them, giving hosts faster feedback. ECN is implemented in many platforms but faces deployment challenges due to blackholes (misconfigured routers). Quick-Start (RFC 4782) allows hosts to request an initial sending rate from routers, accelerating startup compared to slow start.

These mechanisms enable routers to signal congestion state more directly to endpoints, reducing losses and improving performance compared to inference-based methods.
sections.eli5: Instead of just dropping packets when busy, routers can tell senders 'please slow down' with a special mark, and senders can ask 'is it okay if I go fast at first?'

sections.title: Non-TCP and Multicast Approaches
sections.content:
As UDP-based protocols, multimedia streaming, and multicast applications grew, new congestion control mechanisms emerged. SCTP (RFC 4960) adapts TCP-like control for multi-homed connections. TFRC (RFC 5348) provides smoother rate control for streaming, suitable for multimedia. DCCP (RFC 4340) is a framework for unreliable, congestion-controlled datagram delivery.

Multicast congestion control, developed by the Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) Working Group, takes a modular approach using protocol cores and building blocks, with mechanisms like ALC and WEBRC for different multicast scenarios.
sections.eli5: For live video and other special uses, there are different rules that let data flow more smoothly without the stop-and-go pattern TCP uses.
